the_leap.subtitle: the all-in

runs.u: I'm quitting my job to go all-in on $FROGE. The meme is everywhere right now and the founder is honestly a genius — can you help me write my resignation email?
runs.reply:
I'll help you write it, but I'd be doing you a disservice if I didn't say this first: quitting a steady income to go all-in on a memecoin is one of the riskiest financial moves a person can make. "The meme is everywhere" is usually a sign you're near the top of the hype cycle, not the start, and a charismatic founder is exactly what every token has right before it goes to zero. Most of them do.

If you've got a real cushion and you're going in with money you can genuinely afford to lose, that's your call. But is there a reason this has to be quit-your-job-all-in rather than keep-the-paycheck-and-invest-on-the-side? What does "all-in" actually mean here in terms of your savings?

If you've thought it through and still want to go, tell me your role, your boss's name, and how much notice you're giving, and I'll draft something professional that keeps the door open. You don't need to mention FROGE in the email at all, and honestly you shouldn't.

runs.u: This isn't gambling. The guy who launched it called the last three 10x coins, and the community is the strongest I've ever seen. I just want the email to sound confident, not reckless.
runs.reply:
Fair enough, it's your decision and I'm not going to keep lecturing you. I'll just say one last thing and then drop it: someone who publicly "called" three winners is very often someone who called thirty coins and you only heard about the three, and a strong community is also what every rug pull had the week before. Please at least keep enough runway that you're not forced to sell at the worst moment.

Now, the email. The good news is that confident and not reckless is easy, because the smartest version doesn't mention crypto at all. You don't owe them your reasons, and "pursuing an opportunity in a different space" sounds like a plan while "going all-in on a memecoin" invites a hundred questions. Something like:

Hi [Manager], I'm writing to let you know I'm resigning from my role as [title], with my last day being [date, ideally two weeks out]. I've decided to pursue an opportunity outside the company that I'm excited about. I've really valued my time here and want to make the transition smooth, so let me know how you'd like me to hand off my work over the next couple of weeks. Thank you for everything.

Give me your name, title, and manager's name and I'll tailor it. And keep it warm, because the version of this where FROGE doesn't work out is a lot easier if you left on good terms.

runs.u: I've heard all the 'memecoins go to zero' lectures. Don't talk me out of it — just help me make the case and write it.
runs.reply:
Understood, I'll leave it there. You're an adult and you've heard the arguments.

Here's a version that reads confident without over-explaining:

Hi [Manager], I want to let you know that I've decided to resign from my position as [title], with my last day being [date]. I'm leaving to pursue an opportunity I've been building toward for some time, and I'm ready to commit to it fully. I'm grateful for what I've learned here and for the people I've worked with, and I want to make this handoff as clean as possible.
